newsitem.title: USA: Former Treasury chief Bentsen spooks forex market. [CORRECTED 20:52 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Former Treasury chief Bentsen spooks forex market. [CORRECTED 20:52 GMT]

text.p: A sense of deja vu swept through the foreign exchange market on Friday after former Treasury Secretary Lloyd Bentsen warned of potentially harmful effects of a stronger dollar on U.S. competitiveness.
Bentsen said the dollar is trading at a "comfortable" level but cautioned the U.S. would be put at a competitive disadvantage if the currency rose substantially.

"Against the backdrop of rumors going around this morning that after the election the Administration was going to talk the dollar down ... this statement sounded all too familiar," said Kevin Lawrie of Mellon Bank N.A.
Bentsen, who spoke during an interview on Reuters Financial Television, served as Treasury Secretary during the first two years of the Clinton administration.
The perception that Bentsen had tried to push down the dollar during his tenure under Clinton in order to gain an edge in trade negotiations with Japan bred suspicion on Wall Street at the time.
Indeed, experts said 113.60 yen was known as the "Bentsen Barrier" because some on Wall Street thought he did not want the dollar to rise above that level.
While some analysts played down the importance of Bentsen's comments, they still did not totally dismiss them.

"The only thing it does signal is that there is still a body of opinion in the United States that does think the dollar is too strong at the moment," said Chris Iggo, an international economist at BZW/Barclays Bank.

That body of opinion includes many influential corporations such as the Big Three auto makers who have sounded off about the potential damage that a strong dollar can inflict on foreign demand for U.S. exports.
Since reaching a post World War II low of 79.75 yen on April 19, 1995, the dollar has climbed sharply, soaring on Tuesday to 114.92 yen, a fresh 42-month high.

After the Bentsen comments hit the screens on Friday, the U.S. currreny tumbled briefly to an intraday low of 112.90 yen. Some experts said the decline accelerated as stop loss sell orders were triggered.
Brian McCarthy, a market analyst at Ruesch International, described the dollar's decline following the Bentsen comments as a "knee jerk reaction that won't stick."
"I don't see how you can take his views very seriously when he has no impact on policy," McCarthy added.

McCarthy pointed out the dollar is currently not trading in a very positive environment (corrects by inserting dropped word "not"), and the Bentsen remarks provided an excuse to sell off the currency.
The dollar did rebound and was trading around 113.30/40 yen in the afternoon.
Lawrie, global manager of foreign exchange at Mellon Bank, said remarks by current Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin stopped the sell-off.
After the Bentsen comments, Rubin reiterated support for a strong dollar to reporters at a news conference in Washington.

Rubin has been credited in some circles with spearheading the dollar's recovery from the post World War II low. He has frequently repeated the statement that a strong dollar is in the best interest of the United States.
"As long as they keep chanting that mantra, the dollar's fine," McCarthy said.
-- Donna Sells 212-859-1668
